decisions.spanText:
Yep — the cleanest apples-to-apples way is to normalize everything to edible, drained, hydrated corn weight (what you actually eat). Here’s the logic I’m using (this is standard food-science / USDA style normalization):

Frozen corn ≈ already 100% edible

Canned corn ≈ ~60–65% corn solids after draining (rest is water)

Dried corn ≈ ~2.5× weight gain when fully hydrated/cooked


Using that, here’s the normalized table. ---

Normalized comparison (edible, hydrated corn)

Type	Typical retail cost	Normalized cost (per lb edible corn)	Shelf life

Frozen corn	$1.80 / lb	$1.80 / lb edible	8–12 months (freezer)
Canned corn	$0.85 / lb (with liquid)	~$1.35–1.45 / lb edible	3–5 years (pantry)
Dried corn (bulk)	$0.30 / lb (dry)	~$0.12–0.15 / lb edible	1–2 years (pantry, sealed)



---

Why this works

Canned: 1 lb canned → ~0.62 lb actual corn
→ $0.85 ÷ 0.62 ≈ $1.37 per lb edible

Dried: 1 lb dry → ~2.5 lb cooked
→ $0.30 ÷ 2.5 ≈ $0.12 per lb edible

Frozen: already hydrated, no adjustment needed



---

What this means in practice

Canned looks cheap because of water weight — once normalized, it’s only slightly cheaper than frozen, not dramatically. Frozen costs more because of cold-chain logistics, not because the corn itself is expensive. Dried corn absolutely crushes on cost, you pay in:

prep time

texture differences

planning ahead



Rule of thumb

Convenience → frozen

Cheap + easy pantry storage → canned

Ultra-cheap + long-term resilience → dried


If you want, next step could be:

cost per cooked cup

Instant Pot timing + texture outcomes

when dried corn is not worth it (there are cases)
